title: From Abu Dhabi to Gothenburg in 72 Hours: Modi's Five-Nation Blitz Is India's Biggest Diplomatic Bet This Year
excerpt: A $5 billion UAE deal, strategic partnerships with the Netherlands and Sweden, and a pointed message on the Strait of Hormuz — the Prime Minister's whirlwind tour is reshaping India's place in a fracturing world order
body:
In the lexicon of Indian diplomacy, "multi-alignment" has become the defining phrase of the Modi era. This past week, the Prime Minister turned the concept into a masterclass in itinerary planning — touching down in Abu Dhabi, The Hague, and Gothenburg within 72 hours, extracting a $5 billion investment deal from the UAE, signing 17 agreements with the Netherlands, and elevating ties with Sweden to a full strategic partnership. By the time he boards his flight to Oslo for the India-Nordic Summit, Modi will have met three heads of state, addressed European industrialists, and delivered India's clearest message yet on the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

## The UAE stopover: two hours, $5 billion

The Abu Dhabi leg was the shortest — and the most consequential. In a meeting with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan that lasted barely two hours, Modi locked in a package that reads like a wish list: $3 billion for a UAE sovereign wealth fund's acquisition of a stake in RBL Bank, $1 billion earmarked for Sammaan Capital, a new defence cooperation framework, an expansion of India's strategic petroleum reserves by 30 million barrels, and an agreement to build an 8-exaflop AI supercomputer. A ship repair cluster at Vadinar, Gujarat, rounds out the commercial side.

But the geopolitics mattered as much as the economics. With Iranian-backed Houthi drones having struck near the UAE's Barakah nuclear facility days earlier, Modi's condemnation was unambiguous. "The Strait of Hormuz must remain open and free," he said — words that carry weight when 60 per cent of India's crude imports pass through that waterway. The message was aimed as much at Tehran as at Washington: India will defend its energy supply lines, diplomatically if possible, but it will not stay silent.

## The Hague: semiconductors, Chola bronzes, and a delicate dance

In the Netherlands, the agenda was both broader and more nuanced. Modi and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten signed 17 agreements spanning semiconductors, green hydrogen, dairy technology, defence, and critical minerals. The centrepiece was a partnership between Tata Electronics and ASML — the Dutch company whose extreme ultraviolet lithography machines are the chokepoint of global chipmaking — to build capacity at the Dholera Special Investment Region in Gujarat.

For India's semiconductor ambitions, this is a landmark. ASML's technology is subject to export controls that have frozen out China; a formal collaboration signals that the Netherlands views India as a trustworthy node in the West's chip supply chain. A five-year defence roadmap, including joint exercises and counter-terrorism cooperation, added a security dimension to what has traditionally been a trade-focused relationship.

There was also a moment of cultural diplomacy that resonated beyond headlines. The Netherlands returned a set of Chola-era copper plates — temple records dating to the 11th century — to India. The restitution, small in scale, was rich in symbolism, touching the Tamil diaspora in Europe and underlining India's growing leverage in heritage recovery negotiations.

The visit was not friction-free. Jetten raised concerns about press freedom and minority rights in India during a press conference, prompting a crisp rebuttal from India's Ministry of External Affairs. The moment exposed the tension at the heart of these upgraded partnerships: Europe wants India as a geopolitical counterweight to China but cannot fully suppress its instinct to lecture.

## Gothenburg: the Nordic pivot

If the UAE leg was about energy and the Netherlands about technology, Sweden was about the future. Modi and Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson elevated bilateral ties to a strategic partnership — only the third European nation, after France and the Netherlands, to reach that tier with India. A joint action plan for 2026-2030 sets an ambitious target of doubling bilateral trade from the current $7.75 billion. A "Sweden-India Technology Corridor" will connect start-ups and research institutions, while cooperation on AI, critical minerals, and space — including India's Venus Orbiter Mission — points to a relationship moving well beyond IKEA flatpacks and Volvo trucks.

For the 25,000-strong Indian diaspora in Sweden, the visit was a rare moment of visibility. Modi's public reception in Gothenburg drew thousands, many of them IT professionals who have quietly built lives in Scandinavia's tech ecosystem. The strategic partnership formalises what they have long known: India and Sweden share an interest in innovation that their modest trade numbers have never captured.

## What the tour means

Taken together, the three stops tell a coherent story. India is locking in energy insurance in the Gulf, technology supply chains in Europe, and innovation partnerships in Scandinavia — all while the global order fractures along lines that make non-alignment obsolete and multi-alignment essential. The $5 billion UAE deal insulates against oil shocks. The ASML partnership hedges against chip shortages. The Swedish corridor diversifies beyond the traditional Silicon Valley dependence.

For the diaspora — whether they are financial professionals in Dubai, engineers in Eindhoven, or data scientists in Stockholm — these agreements create new professional and commercial corridors. When a prime minister's itinerary can move markets, reassure allies, and recover ancient bronzes in the same week, the diplomatic machinery is firing on all cylinders. Whether the follow-through matches the ambition is, as always, the harder question.
